chapter_title: Developing and Deploying Your First Smart Contract

screens.title: Developing and Deploying Your First Smart Contract
screens.subtitle: A practical lab using Remix, the AdvancedStorage contract, and deployment to a testnet

narration.text: In this lesson you will build, test, and deploy a simple but practical Solidity contract using Remix. We'll move from writing the AdvancedStorage contract to compiling and running it in Remix's JavaScript VM, and then deploy the same contract to a public testnet via MetaMask. This hands-on path makes abstract concepts concrete: you will see how constructor arguments set initial state, how require checks protect functions, and how events let external applications observe changes. Practical practice in Remix reduces friction because it requires no local setup and surfaces compilation errors immediately. By the end you will be able to deploy a contract, call its read and write functions, and interpret revert messages and emitted events. As you work, pay attention to the owner pattern, indexed event fields, and the difference between local simulation and testnet deployment. Who will own the contract you deploy, and what happens if someone else tries to change its state? Keep that question in mind as you begin the lab.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Practically deploying a contract moves you from concept to working DApp components: ownership, events, and secure writes matter for real applications.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you will practice and verify in the lab

narration.text: By the end of this lab you will accomplish four practical objectives that map directly to everyday DApp development tasks. First, you will set up and navigate the Remix IDE so you can author, compile, and debug Solidity contracts without installing tooling. For example, creating a new file and choosing a compatible compiler version removes common configuration headaches. Second, you will write a simple but functional contract, AdvancedStorage, using Solidity types and an owner pattern; this includes declaring state, a constructor, and an event. Third, you will compile the contract and learn to read the compiler output; this skill helps you quickly locate syntax issues like missing semicolons or incorrect types. Finally, you will deploy locally and to a testnet by using the JavaScript VM and an injected provider; deploying with a constructor argument is a common source of deployment errors you will learn to avoid. Each objective builds toward being able to deploy a contract you can interact with and verify, a key milestone for practical blockchain development.

keyIdea.title: Practical competency
keyIdea.text: These objectives ensure you can move from code to a deployed contract, observe events, and troubleshoot common failures.

screens.title: Remix IDE: a browser-based Solidity environment
screens.subtitle: Why Remix is ideal for learning and rapid prototyping

narration.text: Remix is a browser-based Integrated Development Environment tailored for Solidity development. It provides a code editor, a compiler tab that lists errors and warnings, a deploy and run transactions panel, and an integrated terminal. The key practical advantage is zero local setup; you can create a new file, paste your contract, choose a compatible compiler version and immediately compile. For learners, this reduces friction and helps focus on code patterns like constructors, events, and require checks. A concrete example: when you paste AdvancedStorage and select a compiler compatible with pragma 0.8. x, Remix highlights syntax errors and shows a console line for the missing semicolon or type mismatch, allowing you to fix issues line by line. A common misconception is that Remix is only for toy examples—while it is excellent for prototyping, it also connects to injected wallets for real testnet deployment. Key takeaway: mastering Remix means you can iterate fast, observe emitted events, and move confidently from local testing to public testnets. Remix IDE: a browser-based Solidity environment means instant environment, clear compiler feedback, and integration with wallets make remix a practical first ide for solidity.. In practical terms, why remix is ideal for learning and rapid prototyping. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

// Paste this into Remix to test

    uint256 value;

screens.title: AdvancedStorage: contract structure and roles
screens.subtitle: Read the contract: state, constructor, event, and ownership

narration.text: Let's read the AdvancedStorage contract line by line to understand how Solidity expresses state, events, constructors, and access control. The contract declares a private numeric state variable and a public owner address. The constructor takes an initial value and sets the deploying address as owner via msg. sender, so the deployer becomes the authoritative account. The event declaration DataChanged contains an indexed user field to make historical filtering efficient. The setData function stores the old value, performs a require check to ensure only the owner may modify state, updates the data variable, and emits DataChanged with the caller, old value, and new value. A common mistake is misnaming variables inside emit—if you emit a variable not in scope or misspell it, compilation fails. For example, emitting newData when the local variable is named _newData causes an error. The core idea is that constructors set initial state, require enforces runtime checks, and events provide an immutable log that frontends can watch. What will your contract log when the owner calls setData with a new value? AdvancedStorage: contract structure and roles means constructors initialize, require enforces checks, and events record state changes for off-chain observers.. In practical terms, read the contract: state, constructor, event, and ownership. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Contract anatomy
keyIdea.text: Constructors initialize, require enforces checks, and events record state changes for off-chain observers.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › AdvancedStorage Walkthrough
Full contract (abridged for clarity)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract AdvancedStorage {
    uint256 private data; 
    address public owner; 
    event DataChanged(address indexed user, uint256 oldData, uint256 newData);

    constructor(uint256 initialData) {
        data = initialData;
        owner = msg.sender;
    }

    function setData(uint256 _newData) public {
        require(msg.sender == owner, "Only the owner can set the data.");
        uint256 oldData = data;
        data = _newData;
        emit DataChanged(msg.sender, oldData, _newData);
    }

    function getData() public view returns (uint256) { return data; }
}
Note: make sure names used in emit match the actual local and state variables to avoid compilation errors.
Explanation & examples
  • Constructor: runs once and sets initial data and owner using the deploying address.
  • msg.sender: the address that initiated the transaction; used here to assign ownership and log the event source.
  • Event indexing: indexed allows efficient searches for the user field in logs.
Concrete example
If deployer sets initialData to 42, getData returns 42. If the owner calls setData(123), DataChanged is emitted with oldData 42 and newData 123.
Common mistake
Emitting a misspelled variable or forgetting to set constructor args will fail compilation or deployment.

screens.title: Events and emit: logging contract activity
screens.subtitle: How events work and why indexed fields matter

narration.text: Events in Solidity act like lightweight logs that are captured on-chain and can be queried by external applications. They do not change contract state, but they create records that frontends and monitoring tools can listen to. In AdvancedStorage, DataChanged includes an indexed user parameter to make searches for a particular caller efficient. As a concrete example, when the owner calls setData to update the stored value, the contract emits DataChanged with the caller's address, the old value, and the new value; a frontend can subscribe to this event and update its UI when it sees that log. A common misconception is that events are a replacement for persistent state—events are not a substitute for storage since logs are not accessible to contracts during execution. Another practical point: events use less gas than storing equivalent data on-chain, but they are not private and remain available publicly. The takeaway is that events are ideal for signaling off-chain systems without requiring additional storage variables. Events and emit: logging contract activity means use events to notify off-chain listeners of state changes; indexed fields make filtering efficient for uis and tools.. In practical terms, how events work and why indexed fields matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Event purpose
keyIdea.text: Use events to notify off-chain listeners of state changes; indexed fields make filtering efficient for UIs and tools.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Events & emit
What is an event?

An event creates a log entry on the blockchain. External applications listen for these logs to react when contract state changes occur. They are indexed for efficient searching.

Efficiency
Logs cost less than equivalent on-chain storage and are optimized for off-chain consumption.
Searchability
Indexed fields allow event filters by address or other indexed values.
Key Takeaway

Emit events for UI updates and monitoring; do not rely on events as in-contract storage.

Concrete scenario
Imagine a DApp that displays the stored value. When the owner calls setData, the frontend listens for DataChanged and refreshes the visible number. If DataChanged includes the user address as indexed, the frontend can filter only events from a specific account efficiently.
Misconception
Do not assume events replace state. Contracts cannot access event logs during execution; store essential values in state variables if contracts must read them later.

screens.title: Compiling in Remix and troubleshooting errors
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step: choose compiler, compile, read messages, and fix issues

narration.text: Compiling is a frequent source of friction for new smart contract developers, so we will make it methodical. Start by matching the pragma directive to a compatible compiler version in Remix's Solidity Compiler tab. For the AdvancedStorage contract with pragma ^0.8.0, choose a 0.8. x release. Click Compile and read the compiler output; errors include a line number, a message, and often a hint about the problem. Common issues include missing semicolons, incorrect variable names, and type mismatches. When you encounter an error, go to the editor line suggested by the compiler and inspect nearby lines—sometimes the actual mistake is in the previous line. If compilation succeeds but you see warnings, review them; some warnings indicate deprecations that might cause runtime surprises. As a concrete example, if the emit line references newData but your parameter is named _newData, the compiler will point to the emit statement. Fixing the variable name resolves the error. After compilation, the Deploy & Run panel will list your contract and let you provide constructor arguments. This process reduces deployment-time failures and saves testnet gas. Compiling in Remix and troubleshooting errors means match compiler to pragma, read messages carefully, and fix the root cause rather than patching around the symptom.. In practical terms, step-by-step: choose compiler, compile, read messages, and fix issues. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Compilation discipline
keyIdea.text: Match compiler to pragma, read messages carefully, and fix the root cause rather than patching around the symptom.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Compile & Troubleshoot
Compile steps
  1. 1
    Select a compiler version compatible with the pragma line.
  2. 2
    Click Compile and inspect the console for errors and warnings.
  3. 3
    Fix the root cause at the referenced line, then recompile.
  4. 4
    When compilation succeeds, confirm the contract appears in the Deploy panel and provide constructor args if needed.
Common compiler traps
Mismatched pragma, wrong variable names, and unexpected semicolons are the most frequent blockers; the console usually tells you which line to inspect first.
Concrete debugging example
If you see an error pointing to the emit line, compare variable names between the function parameters and the emit call. If _newData is the parameter but emit uses newData, correct the emit to use _newData. Recompile to confirm the error is resolved.
Pro tip
Run small incremental compilations after each change. This isolates the change that introduces an error and makes the console output easier to interpret.

screens.title: Deploying to the JavaScript VM (local testing)
screens.subtitle: A safe environment for rapid testing and iteration

narration.text: The JavaScript VM in Remix provides an in-browser simulated blockchain ideal for quick testing. It comes with several pre-funded accounts so you can send transactions without needing testnet ETH. To deploy AdvancedStorage, open the Deploy & Run Transactions panel and select JavaScript VM (London) as the environment. Choose a default account to act as the deployer, supply an initialData argument for the constructor, and click Deploy. After deployment, the contract appears in the Deployed Contracts list where you can call view functions like getData immediately and run transactions such as setData. To validate access control, switch the account in the panel to a different default account and attempt setData again; it should revert with the require message. The console will show the revert and gas used. This pattern lets you observe successful and failed transactions without incurring gas costs on a real network, which is essential for iterating on access control and event emission before publishing to a public testnet. Deploying to the JavaScript VM (local testing) means validate state changes and access control quickly without spending real or testnet eth, and reproduce both successful and reverted transactions.. In practical terms, a safe environment for rapid testing and iteration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Why use JS VM
keyIdea.text: Validate state changes and access control quickly without spending real or testnet ETH, and reproduce both successful and reverted transactions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Deploy: JavaScript VM
Step-by-step
  1. Select "JavaScript VM (London)" in Deploy & Run Transactions.
  2. Choose a pre-funded account to deploy from.
  3. Provide constructor initialData, e.g., 42, and click Deploy.
  4. Interact with getData and setData in the Deployed Contracts panel.
  5. Switch accounts to test require-based access restrictions and observe revert messages.
Key Takeaway

Use the JS VM to check behaviors that would be expensive on a public network, such as intentional reverts or repeated event emissions.

Concrete example
Deploy AdvancedStorage with initialData 42. Click getData to see 42. Call setData(123) from the owner account to observe DataChanged and updated getData. Switch to a different account and try setData again to see a revert with the require message in the console.
Misconception
Don’t assume JS VM replicates network timing; blocks are simulated instantly and behavior like propagation delays differ from a public testnet.

screens.title: Interacting with a Deployed Contract in Remix
screens.subtitle: Calling view and state-changing functions; reading the terminal

narration.text: Interacting with a deployed contract is how you validate behavioral expectations. After the contract appears under Deployed Contracts, you will see buttons for view functions and input fields for state-changing methods. Start with view methods such as owner and getData; these calls do not consume gas when executed as calls in Remix. For state changes like setData, enter a new value and click the transaction button. In the JavaScript VM this executes instantly, while on a testnet it initiates a signed transaction through MetaMask. Inspect the Remix terminal after each transaction: successful transactions show gas used, the transaction hash, and any emitted events. If a transaction reverts due to a require check, the console presents the revert reason and the gas used until failure; note this gas is still consumed on-chain. A common pitfall is expecting read functions to cost gas when called locally; ensure you use the call option for reading state if you want a free read. The takeaway: reading and writing require different execution paths and cost models, and the Remix terminal is your first source of truth for transaction outcomes.

keyIdea.title: Read vs Write
keyIdea.text: View functions are free reads; state changes trigger transactions that consume gas and may revert, with details shown in the terminal.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Interact with Contract
Reading state

Click owner or getData in the deployed contract to perform a call and read values without spending gas on a call. Calls return the current state as observed by the node.

Example
Calling getData after deployment with initialData 42 should return 42 immediately in the UI.
Pitfall
Calling a view function through a transaction consumes gas unnecessarily. Use the call option for free reads.
Writing state

Enter a new value for setData and send the transaction. Observe the terminal for gas usage, transaction hash, and the emitted DataChanged event details. If the call reverts, the revert message explains why.

Example
If a different account calls setData, the transaction will revert with "Only the owner can set the data." and the terminal will show the revert reason.

screens.title: Deploying to Sepolia with MetaMask
screens.subtitle: Prepare MetaMask, obtain test ETH, and publish your contract

narration.text: Deploying to a public testnet introduces a few extra steps compared with the JavaScript VM. First, install MetaMask and configure it to use the Sepolia network. Acquire testnet ETH from a faucet to pay gas fees. In Remix's Deploy & Run Transactions panel, choose Injected Provider – MetaMask and accept the prompt to connect your wallet. Confirm MetaMask is on Sepolia and displays your testnet balance. With AdvancedStorage selected, supply the constructor initialData, click Deploy, and MetaMask will open a transaction confirmation showing estimated gas. Confirm to broadcast the transaction to Sepolia. Monitor the Remix terminal for the transaction hash, then paste the hash into Sepolia block explorer to follow confirmations. Interactions after deployment require signing through MetaMask, so both setData and getData will use the injected provider. Common mistakes include insufficient test ETH, selecting the wrong network in MetaMask, or forgetting constructor arguments. The key is careful verification before confirming: ensure the account, network, and constructor inputs are correct to avoid failed deployments. Deploying to Sepolia with MetaMask means connect metamask to sepolia, ensure test eth in your wallet, provide constructor args, and confirm the transaction carefully.. In practical terms, prepare metamask, obtain test eth, and publish your contract. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Public deployment checklist
keyIdea.text: Connect MetaMask to Sepolia, ensure test ETH in your wallet, provide constructor args, and confirm the transaction carefully.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Deploy: Sepolia
Deployment steps
  1. Install MetaMask and switch to the Sepolia Test Network.
  2. Request Sepolia test ETH from a faucet and confirm receipt in MetaMask.
  3. In Remix, set Environment to "Injected Provider - MetaMask" and connect the wallet.
  4. Provide constructor argument and click Deploy; confirm the transaction in MetaMask.
  5. Monitor the transaction hash in Remix and verify on Sepolia explorers after confirmation.
Common mistake
Deploying on the wrong network or lacking faucet funds will cause the transaction to fail or be rejected by MetaMask.
Concrete example
Provide initialData 101, click Deploy, and confirm the MetaMask dialog showing gas estimate. After mining, interaction with setData will also require MetaMask confirmations and consume test ETH.
Why it matters
Deploying on a testnet simulates mainnet behavior and helps you verify gas usage, transaction latency, and real wallet interactions before production deployments.

screens.title: JavaScript VM vs. Testnet: differences to watch
screens.subtitle: Why behavior differs and how to validate both environments

narration.text: Understanding the differences between the JavaScript VM and a public testnet is essential to interpret results correctly. The JavaScript VM is a simulated in-browser blockchain with instant block mining and pre-funded accounts, which makes it fast and free for iterative testing. A testnet like Sepolia behaves like mainnet in that transactions are mined by distributed nodes, confirmations take time, and transactions consume real testnet ETH for gas. A concrete consequence is timing: a transaction that appears instantaneous in JS VM may take several seconds or longer to confirm on Sepolia. Another difference concerns external services: testnet deployments can be inspected on a block explorer and are visible to third parties; JS VM state exists only in your browser session. A common misconception is assuming gas estimates and final costs are identical between environments. Gas usage patterns are similar, but price (gwei) and network congestion affect cost and timing. The practical approach is to iterate in JS VM, then deploy to Sepolia for final verification of cost, latency, and integration with wallets. JavaScript VM vs. Testnet: differences to watch means use js vm for speed and sepolia for realistic network behavior and wallet integration testing.. In practical terms, why behavior differs and how to validate both environments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Environment contrast
keyIdea.text: Use JS VM for speed and Sepolia for realistic network behavior and wallet integration testing.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › JS VM vs Testnet
JavaScript VM
  • In-browser simulated blockchain with instant mining.
  • Pre-funded accounts for free testing.
  • State is transient and tied to the browser session.
Sepolia Testnet
  • Real distributed network behavior and real test ETH gas costs.
  • Transactions require confirmations and can be inspected on explorers.
  • Suitable for final verification of wallet integration and gas usage.
Practical advice
Iterate quickly in JS VM and then deploy to Sepolia to verify cost, latency, and integration with MetaMask. Expect timing and gas cost differences, and always confirm constructor inputs before deploying publicly.

screens.title: Troubleshooting deployment and interaction errors
screens.subtitle: Common errors, their causes, and how to fix them

narration.text: This lesson lists the most frequent mistakes students encounter and how to resolve them. First, missing constructor arguments cause the deploy button to fail with a parameter error. The fix is to provide the correct type and value in the constructor input field before deploying. Second, wrong compiler version causes incompatibilities; match the pragma to the compiler or adjust pragma to the version you intend to use. Third, deploying on the wrong network in MetaMask leads to declined transactions—ensure MetaMask and Remix are on the same network and that you have test ETH. Fourth, forgetting to switch accounts when testing access control results in confusing behavior—explicitly change the selected account to simulate non-owner calls and observe the revert. Fifth, misspelled variable names in emit or function calls lead to compilation failures; check variable scope and names. For each issue, reproduce it in the JS VM, fix the source, recompile, and then attempt testnet deployment. This stepwise validation uncovers the root cause instead of masking errors with superficial changes. Troubleshooting deployment and interaction errors means reproduce failures locally, correct the root cause, and only then attempt public testnet deployment to avoid wasting test eth.. In practical terms, common errors, their causes, and how to fix them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Fix by replication
keyIdea.text: Reproduce failures locally, correct the root cause, and only then attempt public testnet deployment to avoid wasting test ETH.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Troubleshooting
Error checklist
  • Missing constructor arg: Provide correct type and value at deploy time.
  • Compiler mismatch: Align pragma and compiler selection before compiling.
  • Wrong MetaMask network: Confirm network and wallet balance to avoid failed transactions.
  • Access control confusion: Switch accounts to verify require behavior produces expected reverts.
  • Emit or variable misspellings: Check declaration and use of variable names carefully.
Quick fixes
Reproduce the issue in JS VM, fix the source, recompile, and test interactions locally before deploying to Sepolia. This minimizes wasted testnet ETH and clarifies the root cause of failures.

screens.title: Lab walkthrough: deploy AdvancedStorage to Sepolia
screens.subtitle: Step sequence and challenge to verify ownership and events

narration.text: This lab sequence pulls together everything you have learned. Step one: open Remix and create AdvancedStorage. sol, pasting the provided code and selecting a compiler in the 0.8. x family. Step two: compile and confirm no errors. Step three: on the JavaScript VM, deploy with initialData such as 42 and verify getData returns the value and setData emits DataChanged when called by the owner. Step four: switch accounts in the JS VM to demonstrate that setData reverts for non-owners and inspect the revert reason. Step five: install MetaMask, acquire Sepolia test ETH from a faucet, and switch MetaMask to Sepolia. Step six: in Remix select Injected Provider and connect; provide a constructor argument and deploy via MetaMask, confirming the gas estimate. Step seven: after the transaction is mined, interact with the contract via MetaMask to setData and observe events in the Remix terminal and on the block explorer. Challenge: try calling setData from a second MetaMask account and observe the revert and the gas consumed. This lab verifies ownership, events, and the full deployment lifecycle. Lab walkthrough: deploy AdvancedStorage to Sepolia means deploy locally, then to sepolia, and demonstrate that only the owner can change stored data while events log each successful update.. In practical terms, step sequence and challenge to verify ownership and events. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Events, access control, and common Solidity primitives

narration.text: This final summary highlights Solidity primitives and patterns you practiced. The msg. sender global variable identifies the caller of a function and is essential for owner patterns and access control. The require function enforces runtime checks and reverts transactions when conditions fail; remember that revert still consumes gas up to the failure point. Events and the emit keyword produce logs that off-chain systems can filter and react to; indexed fields make searching efficient. MetaMask acts as an injected provider so you can sign transactions from your browser when deploying to Sepolia. Finally, faucets supply test ETH needed for public testnet transactions. Together these concepts form the core of safe and verifiable smart contract deployment and interaction practices. Keep testing locally, verify events, and always double-check constructor arguments and network settings before you confirm a transaction.

Events & emit
